items.abstract: <jats:p>The growing complexity of modern network infrastructures demands automation solutions that are not limited to the static scripting and traditional Software-Defined Networking (SDN) controllers. In this paper, a new, decentralized, Agentic AI, model of network engineering is presented, designed to provide intent-aware auto-remediation and active optimization. The proposed system makes use of a set of specialized autonomous agents, powered by Local Large Language Models (LLMs) and anchored by Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) to read higher-level human intentions, validate them, and implement amendments. The paper introduces a strong Human-in-the-Loop architecture where the critical actions are first checked by a network simulation engine (Batfish) [2] and then approved by operators before being deployed. Its implementation, tested in resource-constrained environments, shows a feasible path towards the implementation of "NetDevOps" by integrating a Source of Truth (NetBox), Observability (Prometheus [6] / Loki), and Workflow Orchestration (n8n). The experimental findings validate the fact that the system can convert intent in natural language into valid network configurations that can support agent response times of less than 15ms and hence agility and reliability in network operations.</jats:p>
title: "The Era of AI Agents for Network Engineering": Intent-Aware Auto Remediation for Network Disruption or Failures Using AI Agents, Large Language Models (LLM) and Model Context Protocol (MCP) Mechanisms

items.abstract: <jats:p>Networking industry is changing fast, with the complexity growing with the implementation of cloud computing, the Internet of things, and multi-vendor environments (Oswalt et al., 2023). Manual and semiautomated approaches to network management lack the capability to support the rigorous demands of real-time decision-making, scalability and responsiveness to dynamic situations. In this paper, a conference proposal has been presented, and it suggests a holistic framework that incorporates the Model Context Protocol (MCP), large language models (LLMs), retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), and autonomous AI agents, as a means of network management. Human-in-the-loop controls are provided in the framework to maintain compliance with regulatory and organizational requirements.     We created an ecosystem which integrates specialized  AI agents - Routing, Optimization, Implementation,  Monitoring, and Notification - coordinated through n8n  and anchored through Retrieval-Augmented Generation  (RAG) to provide factual accuracy in accordance with  enterprise network spaces. The system converts  operator intent in managing networks into verified  network settings, performs proactive optimization and  maintains audit trails, thus ensuring that enterprise  networks perform optimally.  This study adds value to the research area by showing  how machine-learning and LLM based techniques can be  practically applied to end-to-end network operations as  the blueprint to reliable autonomous networking. In  addition, this paper stresses that there are certain  computing requirements required to implement and  maintain an ecosystem of this kind.</jats:p>
title: A Design Science Approach for Agentic AI in Network Engineering: Autonomous Network Management Using AI Agents, Large Language Models (LLM) And Model Context Protocol (MCP) Mechanisms

items.abstract: <jats:p>The Model Context Protocol (MCP) has moved from a connectivity convention into shared infrastructure for agentic systems: models discover natural-language tool descriptions, retrieve resources, call external services, and increasingly act under real user identities. That interoperability creates a distinctive security problem. MCP carries both semantic influence and operational capability across boundaries that conventional application security normally separates. A malicious descriptor can steer a model before a tool is called; a legitimate tool can be composed with a second capability to exfiltrate data; an authorization implementation can accept the wrong token or protocol version; and an ordinary server bug can become remotely reachable through an AI agent that supplies attacker-controlled arguments. We synthesize the MCP specification and security guidance, peer-reviewed and preprint research, benchmarks, and representative public vulnerability disclosures through 8 August 2026. We introduce MCP-SEC-28, a systems taxonomy containing 28 failure modes across seven families: metadata and semantic integrity; authentication, authorization, and consent; protocol, transport, and discovery; execution and local environment; supply chain and server provenance; composition and cross-server trust; and observability, containment, and recovery. We then analyze how attacks cross these families, map empirical evidence and public CVEs to the taxonomy, and assess the security implications of the 2026-07-28 MCP specification, including its stateless core, header-based routing, cacheable catalog results, authorization hardening, extensions, and deprecations. The central conclusion is that MCP security cannot be reduced to prompt-injection filtering or OAuth correctness alone. Safe deployment requires signed and versioned capability metadata, strict resourcebound identity, deterministic policy enforcement, origin and network controls, semantic validation, least privilege, sandboxing, transaction boundaries, independent verification, and end-to-end provenance. MCP should be treated as an execution supply chain whose natural-language control surface is adversarial by default.&nbsp;</jats:p>
title: MCP Under Attack: Security Risks in the Model Context Protocol Ecosystem

WebMCP Security and the Authenticated Attack Surface

items.abstract: <jats:p>The Model Context Protocol (MCP) enables AI agents to interact with external tools but enlarges the attack surface to prompt injection, tool poisoning, privilege escalation, remote code execution, data exfiltration, and supply-chain risks. Existing defenses such as TLS, authentication, and heuristics protect communication but leave post-decryption behavior ungoverned. We propose the Zero-Trust Proof-Gated Agent Architecture (ZPAA), which treats large language models (LLMs) as untrusted proposers. ZPAA enforces defensein-depth through a minimal action DSL verified by a deterministic policy engine, single-use capability tokens, sandboxed execution with strict guards, and layered validation via DLP, schema gates, and provenance checks. Audit logs ensure observability and tamper resistance. Contributions include: (1) a taxonomy of MCP vulnerabilities, (2) ZPAA design separating proposal from authority, (3) capability token formalization with a verifying interpreter, and (4) an evaluation framework. Results show ZPAA blocks major MCP attack classes, reducing residual risk to LLM fallibility and rare systemlevel exploits.</jats:p>
title: Zero-Trust Proof-Gated Agent Architecture (ZPAA): A Comprehensive Security Model for the Model Context Protocol (MCP)
